HEADLINE: La Trobe kicks off RMBS
TEXT:
Non-bank lender La Trobe Financial has its second residential mortgage-backed security transaction for 2017 in the works, according to sources.

Street Talk understands the deal is being pitched to investors at $350 million to $500 million in size. It follows a $300 million transaction earlier this year.

The RMBS issue, targeted for September, is part of La Trobe's overall funding mix which also includes institutional term facilities and its own credit fund.

It comes as the non-bank lending market continues to benefit from a retreat by the major banks in several areas including interest-only mortgages and lending to foreigners.

La Trobe, which was founded by Ray O'Neill in 1952, was last year in the crosshairs of ASX-listed MyState, before negotiations fell over.

Elsewhere in capital markets, the ASX's newest stock, Elmo Software Ltd, finished its first day on the boards up 25 per cent on Thursday.

At a time when IPO candidates are dropping like flies, Elmo raised $25 million at $2 a share for a $108.3 million market capitalisation via lead manager Wilsons, and finished its first day's trade at $2.50.

HEADLINE: TOT spells trouble for 360 Capital's Tony Pitt
TEXT:
There's trouble on the home front for property fund predator Tony Pitt just as he lines up his next target.

This week Pitt, who has a fearsome reputation for getting his way with resistant property funds, announced his ambition to kick out the management of Asia Pacific Data Centres and run the fund himself.

It is the first big corporate move he's made since creating a property funds empire and selling most of it to Centuria late last year.

He retained the $76 million 360 Capital Total Return Fund. The TOT fund, as its ticker is, is a tidy little treasure chest for Tony, but it has some unhappy campers inside.

Among them is Aurora, which is backed by controversial activist investor Nick Bolton, and private equity powerhouse CVC.

They are among the shareholders who are not happy with an equity raising in April and worried there is more to come.

CVC is particularly aggrieved by Pitt's plans to push his platform into mezzanine debt lending. That's a business CVC is already in, so it must seem a bit rich, from their perspective, to be investing in competitor.

Between them CVC and the Bolton-backed Aurora have enough clout to call a meeting in the hope of persuading fellow investors to order a wind-up.

Taking a lunge at a big target is something Bolton has tried before - hello BrisConnections! - but he may not have dealt with anyone as resolute as Pitt before.

Watching the drama unfold will be Melbourne-based fund manager APN Property.

That's because Pitt's platform, effectively through the TOT fund, has an 18 per cent stake in an APN-run listed industrial fund.

That's enough to make APN nervous enough, even though they have a bigger stake in the industrial fund, and happy to see Pitt now has his own distraction to deal with.

HEADLINE: BAML sends teaser for ALS asset care unit
TEXT:
Bank of America Merrill Lynch has wasted no time in seeking a buyer for ALS Ltd's asset care business, sending a teaser document to interested parties and asking more serious tyre-kickers to sign confidentiality agreements ahead of an auction.

The bankers have pitched ALS's up-for-sale unit as a leading provider of asset reliability and integrity services to industrial asset owners, operators, constructors and manufacturers.

Interested parties were told that it is a market leader in Australia with national coverage, and was positioned for growth in the United States' gulf coast and south-east Asia.

According to the teaser document obtained by Street Talk, ALS's asset care business had $141 million revenue and $18 million earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation in the 2017 financial year, mostly from clients in the power, mining and oil and gas industries.

Those three industries account for more than three-quarters of the business' revenue, while services include risk-based inspection and maintenance strategies, fitness for service inspections and materials and mechanical testing.

Interested parties were told the unit has about 600 permanent employees operating in 12 sites across Australia and another five on the US gulf coast.

The bankers also flagged the unit's safety record and management team, and spruiked its "significant growth opportunities".

The unit is pitched at potential trade and private equity buyers, and an auction is expected to be up and running as early as next month.

The flyer comes hot on the heels of ALS Ltd announcing it was evaluating strategic options for the business unit following inbound inquiries. It has hired BAML to test the market more widely.

Sell-side analysts said selling the unit would be in line with ALS Ltd's strategy to move more towards lab testing businesses and away from field services. Macquarie analysts said it was likely to attract interest from global asset care players including Mistras, Acuren, Applus and Bureau Veritas.

Deutsche Bank analysts reckon the unit is worth $132 million to $170 million, or seven-to-nine times historical EBITDA.

The potential divestment also comes as ALS Ltd nears a deal to sell its oil and gas business, expected to be worth about $100 million.

HEADLINE: Ceres Agriculture fattened up and ready for the market
TEXT:
NSW-based Ceres Agricultural Company has quietly kicked off a sale process which has piqued the interest of offshore and domestic suitors.

Street Talk understands cattle station operator North Australian Pastoral Company (NAPCo), which is majority owned by QIC, and a separate group which includes the Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan, are among a handful of would-be bidders for Ceres.

Colliers International has already overseen site visits in recent weeks and expressions of interest are said to be due in early to mid July.

Ceres operates 15 properties throughout the central tablelands and north-west slopes of NSW, according to its website.

Among those are 'Mayfield' and 'Ballyroe' at Oberon; 'Gunyerwarildi', 'Postmans', 'Brentwood', 'Lava Downs' and 'Inverness' at Warialda.

It may fetch a price tag of $200 million to $250 million and the auction is expected to wrap up in three to four months.

The business has diverse operations which span 30,000 hectares of Australian grazing and cropping land.

Its website says Ceres operates in logistics, feed mill, is the largest supplier of "supplementary grain fed premium" beef, a major producer of grains, pulses, oilseeds and superfine merino wool.

Ceres is majority owned by former stockbroker turned property entrepreneur Garrick Hawkins, who last year settled a dispute with the Australian Tax Office.

The potential Ceres sale also comes as private equity behemoth Terra Firma weighs a sale of cattle group Consolidated Pastoral Company.

It's an interesting time to be selling as industry conditions have improved in the past 12 months, including a rise in asset values and shortage in beef stocks.

Foreign buyers of either asset would need to apply to the Foreign Investment Review Board for approval.

Elsewhere, APP Securities is re-stocking its ranks and is said to have made six hires.

In corporate finance, APP has hired former Cabral Resources managing director and JPMorgan banker Michael Bogue and Sydney Capital Partners' Stuart Anderson.

In institutional sales, Colin Silver, who has had stints at ABN Amro and Deutsche Bank, and former Systematix and JPMorgan operative Jitendra Marchino have joined. APP has also started an Asia desk with two new hires.

Also in people moves, and as first reported by Street Talk, CLSA gaming analyst Sacha Krien has resigned from the firm to take up a post at Tabcorp, .

Melbourne-based Krien is said to be joining Tabcorp in an investor relations and corporate strategy role. CLSA plans to replace him.

HEADLINE: Wesfarmers cleans up Officeworks capital structure
TEXT:
If Wesfarmers ever makes another attempt to offload office supplies retailer Officeworks through a trade sale or initial public offering the process should be a little easier.

ASIC documents lodged this week show that Officeworks went ahead with the buy-back of $87 million redeemable preference shares held by The Coles Group (AKA Wesfarmers) on June 14, almost a month after deciding to pull the pin on a $1.5 billion initial public offering.

The buy-back was aimed at simplifying Officeworks' capital structure ahead of a float and removing Coles Group from any transaction as the formal owner of the shares.

Officeworks and Wesfarmers decided to complete the buy-back despite abandoning the IPO, thereby making any sale or float easier in the future. The buy-back will have no impact on Officeworks' accounts, with the reduction in cash offset by a reduction in liabilities.

Wesfarmers was looking for about $1.5 billion for Officeworks and would be lucky to achieve that price in today's market, given the derating in retail stocks due to fears about Amazon's impact.

While the Officeworks sale may be dead for the time being, private equity has not lost its appetite for office suppliers both in Australia and offshore. On Wednesday night, American buyout firm Sycamore Partners agreed to buy US-listed Staples for $US6.9 billion.

Back in Australia, the No.2 and No.3 players Staples Australia and OfficeMax were snapped up by Platinum Equity earlier this year. The competition regulator is due to rule on that tie-up next month.

HEADLINE: Banks want Marshall to kill SA tax
TEXT:
The fate of the $370 million bank tax in South Australia looks like being determined by the state's Liberal opposition leader Steven Marshall.

Fortunately, Marshall is a former businessman who must understand the importance of predictable and rational taxation policies in order to encourage investment and create jobs.

Before going into politics, Marshall worked for his father's successful furniture company, Marshall Furniture, and as a textiles manager at South Australian wool company Michell.

Experience in business would have given Marshall a good understanding of the role played by banks in financing economic growth. They are the grease that keeps the economic machine running smoothly.

It is staggering that Premier Jay Weatherill and Treasurer Tom Koutsantonis don't understand the unintended consequences of their move against the banks. Koutsantonis described it as a "super profits tax" deliberately targeted at the banks because they make about $30 billion a year.

He ignored the fact that relative to the equity investment, there is nothing unusual about the profits made by the banks. In terms of return on equity they are middle of the pack when benchmarked against the top 100 companies.

Koutsantonis this week stepped up his attack on the banks but his allegations about fee gouging were plain wrong.

The fact is the tax has no relationship to the size or profitability of the banks' operations in South Australia. It applies to liabilities that are not even domiciled or sourced from the state.

It is early days but the word out of Adelaide is that the big four banks are gaining traction with their grassroots campaign to convince the local community that the tax is a bad idea.

The campaign steps up a gear today and at the weekend when the Australian Bankers Association's anti-bank tax advertising campaign moves from newspapers to radio and television. The campaign has been accompanied by targeted media appearances in Adelaide by senior bank executives, most notably ANZ Banking Group chief executive Shayne Elliott.

Elliott, who met with Weatherill and Koutsantonis as well as Marshall and members of SA's upper house, has been highly effective in getting the message out about the damage that the tax will cause to the state's economy.

Another executive active in the Adelaide media this week was Andrew Hagger, an Adelaide boy who is now chief customer officer, consumer and wealth at National Australia Bank. He reminded South Australians the bank tax was a tax on investment and would have a negative impact on capital expenditure in the state.

Elliott from ANZ backed up his strong comments by selling out of tens of millions of dollars of South Australian government issued bonds. As a result, the spreads on the bonds widened this week.

Elliott knows as well as every other bank CEO that if the banks lose the anti-tax campaign in South Australia then the tax will spread to other states, with Western Australia the likely next domino to fall.

The mechanics of how the tax spread from Canberra to Adelaide was summed up well on Thursday by BHP chairman Jac Nasser at a business lunch in Sydney.

In response to a question from Chanticleer, Nasser said Australia would not have the bank tax in South Australia if there had not been a federal bank tax by Morrison.

"I just think this just isn't sound policy," he said. "You can't take sectors and start slicing them up and saying they're doing well and we are going to punish the people who are doing well.

"If they don't like the regulatory framework or if they don't like the policies or if there is something fundamentally askew in the banking sector, they should fix that, not just keep taxing."

Westpac Banking Corp chief executive Brian Hartzer, who was in Melbourne on Thursday for a Westpac 200th anniversary event, said he believed a majority of South Australians could see the tax was "bad for jobs and bad for investment in South Australia".

When asked about staff morale, Hartzer said: "Certainly many of our staff are questioning why it is that politicians seem to think going after banks is such a good idea when they know how hard they are working to support their customers."

It will not be easy for Marshall to take a stand against the tax. The Liberal party would have to block supply by opposing the budget in both the lower and upper houses in South Australia.

Blocking the tax in the upper house will require the support of independent members of the legislative council.

Marshall has said he is opposed to the tax but has stopped short of saying he would block the budget.

The Liberal party will hold a party room meeting on Monday. But we may not know Marshall's position until he stands up in parliament on Tuesday to deliver his budget in reply speech.

Slaters: a rolled gold disaster

When control of law firm Slater + Gordon this week moved into the hands of hedge funds specialising in distressed debt, it closed the penultimate chapter in a rolled gold corporate disaster.

A legal firm formed 79 years ago to service the needs of unions and working people lost sight of its true purpose after listing on the stock exchange a decade ago.

Profit growth became the top priority at SGH. Incentives were put in place which encouraged lawyers to generate as much work in progress (WIP) as possible.

Accounting standards allowed SGH to recognise revenue over the life of a case using a stage of completion basis. A corresponding WIP asset was recognised on the balance sheet. This business model apparently worked well for many years after the listing in May 2007.

But rapid growth in SGH's revenue and equally rapid expansion in current and non-current balances of WIP set off alarm bells among astute investors.

Dispassionate analysis of SGH's accounts raised doubts about the model. It seemed that the WIP current assets were not being converted into cash. Either the WIP should have been classified as non-current or impaired.

These issues were just bubbling to the surface when CEO Andrew Grech bet the company on a $1.22 billion acquisition of the professional services division of Quindell in the United Kingdom. This was funded with a combination of debt and an $890 million equity issue.

The Quindell assets were entirely written off within 18 months.

The Quindell deal raised doubts about the quality of advice received, the standard of due diligence and the governance of SGH.

SGH chairman John Skippen did not respond well to criticism of the company and its strategy. He fell into the trap of blaming short sellers of the stock for the company's woes.

The main bankers to SGH, Westpac Banking Corp and National Australia Bank, wrote down their debt. But initially they provided a life line to the company, which avoided writing the debt off so soon after handing it over.

The hedge funds that now own the company are led by Anchorage Capital, which has a history of making money from distressed debt purchases in Australia. They can start with a clean slate because Grech is leaving, as is the entire board of directors.

SGH has not been well understood by the sharemarket. The stock was bid up last year when it was obvious SGH's dire debt situation would destroy the company's equity holders.

On Thursday, there was a similar level of misplaced optimism. The stock was trading about 9¢ a share even though the entire issued capital will shrink to 5 per cent of the recapitalised company.

SGH still has about $550 million of WIP on its balance sheet. That is likely to be worthless because every decent case would already have been turned to cash.

The final chapter of this inglorious episode in the history of SGH will be written when Anchorage turns the business around. But that could take many years.

HEADLINE: Dishing up restaurant empires
TEXT:
Merivale boss Justin Hemmes, top, and celebrity chef Neil Perry, right, are the faces of the next big trend: the rise of high-end restaurant conglomerates, including one that's eyeing a $1 billion ASX listing. But is it good for the food - and us, the diners?

HEADLINE: Project turf wars are senseless
TEXT:
Turf wars within the Turnbull government have sidelined Infrastructure Australia and weakened the nation's project pipeline, says shadow infrastructure minister Anthony Albanese, despite industry participants welcoming the creation of a new financing agency.

"It's absurd that you have two ministers and a renamed parliamentary secretary here yesterday - who's in charge? No one," Mr Albanese told The Australian Financial Review National Infrastructure Summit in Sydney on Thursday.

Infrastructure Minister Darren Chester, Urban Infrastructure Minister Paul Fletcher and Assistant Cities Minister Angus Taylor all addressed the Summit on Wednesday.

The creation of an Infrastructure and Project Financing Agency (IPFA) in the Department of Prime Minster and Cabinet, separated both from Infrastructure Australia and the Department of Infrastructure, was a "diabolical idea", Mr Albanese said.

Labor has pledged to scrap the IPFA if elected and use the money to re-establish a "major cities unit" in Infrastructure Australia.

Mr Taylor on Thursday defended the IPFA, saying the government needed people who knew how to attract more capital into infrastructure. "There is a wall of money wanting to get into transport infrastructure projects. What we don't have is projects being structured in a clever way by the federal government to attract that.

"We have not, in this country, invested in public transport infrastructure with private sector finance on the scale that is necessary now to get these sorts of projects up. We need private sector capital coming in. To be a financier - which we have to be - without having financial skills and capacity is mad. That's what Albo is proposing. He says economists are going to be investors. I love economists - that's my background - but they're not investors.

"We need people who know how to attract capital, how to structure projects to attract capital at a pace and on a scale that we have never done before."

Mr Albanese argues that under the former Labor government, Infrastructure Australia had helped develop projects with the private sector, including the Gold Coast light rail system, G:link, but that the Turnbull government had cleared its board of "dangerous radicals" such as businessman Rod Eddington, Moorebank Intermodal Company chairman Kerry Schott and IFM Investors chairman Garry Weaven.

Dr Schott told the summit on Thursday it was a "curious decision" to put the new financing unit in the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet rather than in Infrastructure Australia.

Paul Oppenheim, chief executive of infrastructure developer Plenary, said the group was "open-minded" about the IPFA and encouraged the federal government to consult on how to best focus the agency.

Garry Bowditch, executive director with the University of Sydney's John Grill Centre for project leadership, said the establishment of the IPFA was a sign that Infrastructure Australia's focus on project risk had been "underwhelming".

"The idea of just dropping money on a project and then leaving it has left us with projects which are really not relevant to what Australia needs."

The IPFA would be useful if it made the government scrutinise the long-term performance of infrastructure assets more closely, but it should be located in Treasury or the Department of Finance, Mr Bowditch said.

"I think the industry has got too used to having lazy cash given to them without the accountabilities of performing."

Steve Lambert, executive general manager of capital financing at NAB, said the new unit would not be useful if it undertook only projects that could be done by the private sector.

"Our first question of the agency is how does it work with Infrastructure Australia and where are the skills and also how does it work with the states?"

The new agency was not likely to increase the price of private sector debt, but it would make it harder for the private sector to get the volumes of deals they would like, Mr Lambert said.

There was no problem getting financing or funding for infrastructure projects, he added. "We see a lot of interest not just from domestic banks and fund managers but also from overseas investors in quality projects.

"The challenge is always around quality projects, trying to find them - there's a lot of competition in the market."

HEADLINE: Power price wave slams business
TEXT:
A destructive wave of energy bill increases is poised to sweep across businesses and households from July 1, and some commercial customers will be hit by a tripling in electricity prices after the closure of the Hazelwood coal generator.

The news of the price increase coincides with a sudden escalation of concern over the overstretched east coast gas market after the unexpected shutdown of a major offshore platform in the Bass Strait just before a cold snap in the south-east.

The shutdown has cut gas supply from the biggest supply source for the east coast by 15 per cent and triggered a sharp spike in wholesale gas tariffs, underscoring the pressures being felt across the energy sector.

Businesses coming off multi-year electricity contracts signed when the power market was in oversupply will suffer worst in the wave of retail price increases, seeing jumps in their total energy bills that will dwarf the up to 20 per cent rise some households face.

Victoria-based Wilson Transformer Co is preparing for an 83 per cent surge in its annual power bill from about $800,000 to almost $1.5 million, including a more-than-threefold jump in the electricity component of the charge, said executive chairman Robert Wilson. Its price for peak power is going from just under 4.4¢ a kilowatt-hour to about 15.4¢, while its off-peak tariff will jump from just over 2.5¢/kWh to about 9.65¢.

"It's been a shock," Mr Wilson said. "We can't change our prices because we are an import-export competing business so it's just straight off the bottom line."

Mr Wilson and other consumers blame the shutdown by French-owned Engie in March of its 1600-megawatt brown coal Hazelwood plant in the Latrobe Valley for the price increases. The closure removed a big source of low-cost baseload power from the market and made much dearer gas-fired generation the price setter across the wholesale market, sending prices soaring.

"We all know it's a dirty old brown coal power station but the reality is, it shouldn't have been closed so dramatically quickly; it's just disrupted the market," Mr Wilson said.

Hazelwood is only part of the story of the dramatic transformation in the power market since Wilson Transformer took out its last electricity purchasing contract, said Jon Stretch, chief executive of ERM Power, which had supplied the Melbourne-based power transformer manufacturer before losing the contract to Origin in the past few weeks.

"That's the period where we've seen this incredible increase in the wholesale market; it doesn't matter which retailer you are talking to," Mr Stretch said, pointing to the shutdown of Alinta's Northern coal generator in South Australia and other coal plants, which has cut the supply of baseload power and increased reliance on intermittent renewables.

Contract prices for commercial customers are based on the forward market on the day they are signed so increases in wholesale tariffs go straight through on the contracts, Mr Stretch noted.

While the hit to businesses from higher electricity and gas prices has been making headlines all year, so far it's only the tip of the iceberg that has been evident, with a whole lot more to come, said Ivan Slavich, chief executive of electricity procurement advisor Energy Action.

"My guess would be that only 20 or 30 per cent of business have really felt it," Mr Slavich said.

"It's those electricity and gas customers that are coming off contract, that's when they get impacted. They may have signed a deal back in 2012 or 2013 for a five year contract and it's only now coming up for renewal."

He said one of the bigger clients of Energy Action, which advises Wilson, was looking at a $12 million increase in its annual power bill to $32 million, one of several increases set to hit in the new financial year.

The unexpected shutdown of the Marlin B platform owned by Esso-BHP Billiton is meanwhile fraying nerves on supply just as the southern states head into the coldest weeks of the year when gas demand peaks in Victoria.

A drop in scheduled production from Esso-BHP's Longford gas plant from 802 terajoules a day to about 640 TJ/d caused the Victoria wholesale gas price to just from $9.51 a gigajoule to $15.82 a gigajoule, said Josh Stabler, managing director of trader EnergyEdge.

"It's just a really important asset, supplying in the order of 50 per cent of the southern market, so any hiccups at Longford are a major issue for the market," Mr Stabler said.

"For the first kind of really big demand today, losing a quarter of Longford would be pretty painful."

An Esso spokesman said the platform had been hit by an electrical fault and couldn't say when it would be rectified.

Mr Slavich said he was surprised more businesses hadn't been more aggressive in acting to limit the impact of rising energy bills by improving their power management and installing on-site generation such as solar panels.

"The tide's gone out, there's a tsunami on the horizon. I'm surprised more people are not running for the high country," he said. "Once the tsunami hits you are now playing catch-up, as to initiate a reduction in energy usage takes time, it doesn't happen overnight. Businesses should be absolutely doing that now."

Federal Energy Minister Josh Frydenberg said the Turnbull government was taking immediate action to put downward pressure on power prices" and ensure reliable supply, pointing to the three measures announced by the Prime Minister last week.

HEADLINE: Barnaba quits Macquarie for RBA board
TEXT:
Prominent West Australian businessman Mark Barnaba has resigned as Macquarie Capital's head of global resources and will take up a coveted position on the board of the Reserve Bank.

Mr Barnaba, a director of Fortescue Metals Group and former chairman of AFL club West Coast Eagles, will join the nine-member RBA board on August 31, when he will also depart Macquarie.

He replaces John Akehurst.

Treasurer Scott Morrison said Mr Barnaba's appointment would ensure the RBA retained a West Australian perspective.

"It was 10 years ago that my predecessor Peter Costello appointed Mr Akehurst to the Reserve Bank Board to ensure the West Australian perspective was understood in the board's important deliberations, a perspective that will continue with Mr Barnaba's appointment," Mr Morrison said.

Mr Barnaba declined to comment.

Under the Reserve Bank Act, a board member is not permitted to be a director, officer or employee of an Authorised Deposit-taking Institution.

As well as steering its global resources business, Mr Barnaba is the face of Macquarie in WA. He has been Macquarie WA chairman since 2012.

Macquarie chief executive Nicholas Moore wrote to staff yesterday advising them of Mr Barnaba's departure.

"On joining Macquarie in February 2012 Mark was appointed chairman of our Western Australian business, with the mission to further expand our Western Australian operations," Mr Moore wrote.

"Under Mark's leadership our Perth office has grown significantly with Macquarie Group invested capital in Western Australia having nearly doubled to over $8 billion in that time."

Macquarie executive director Abe Anad will become head of the Perth office.

Mr Barnaba is the third West Australian to secure a prominent national role this year. Outgoing Wesfarmers chief executive Richard Goyder was appointed chairman of the AFL in February and James Edelman was appointed to the High Court of Australia in January.

Mr Morrison said Mr Akehurst, whose second term ends on August 30, had "made an outstanding and important contribution to Reserve Bank Board deliberations through a challenging period for the Australian economy".

"I thank him for his exceptional service over the past decade. I wish him every success for the future," Mr Morrison said.

Mr Barnaba is also chairman of the University of Western Australia's business school board and the Black Swan Theatre Company.
